content: Tanning addiction is a rare condition in which an individual develops a physical and/or psychological dependency on sunbathing or the use of tanning beds. The exact mechanism underlying this addiction remains unknown. In 2005, dermatologists conducted a study that revealed frequent tanners often lose control over their tanning habits, exhibiting behaviors similar to those seen in individuals addicted to smoking or alcohol. Biochemical evidence suggests that tanning addicts may be dependent on the release of opioids that occurs during tanning. A 2006 study demonstrated that frequent tanners who were given an endorphin blocker experienced severe withdrawal symptoms, whereas infrequent tanners did not exhibit any withdrawal symptoms under the same conditions. The term tanorexia is often used to describe a condition where individuals engage in excessive outdoor sun tanning or overuse other tanning methods, such as tanning beds, in an effort to achieve a darker skin tone because they perceive themselves as unacceptably pale. While tanorexia and tanning addiction may overlap, they are distinct conditions, though both could be considered subsets of tanning addiction. The term tanorexia has been popularized by the media and some medical professionals, but it has not been widely accepted within the medical community and is often regarded as slang. The term was inspired by anorexia nervosa, a condition characterized by low body weight, distorted body image, and an obsessive fear of gaining weight. Severe cases of tanorexia can pose significant health risks, as many popular tanning methods involve prolonged exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation, a known cause of adverse effects such as skin cancer. In extreme cases, tanorexia may be indicative of body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), a mental health condition in which individuals are excessively critical of their physical appearance to an obsessive and compulsive degree. Similar to individuals with anorexia nervosa, who may perceive themselves as overweight despite being underweight, those with tanorexia may believe they have a much lighter or paler complexion than they actually do, even when their skin is already quite dark. Although tanorexia has not been officially recognized or described by the medical community, reported symptoms include intense anxiety when a tanning session is missed, competitive behavior among peers to achieve the darkest tan, and chronic dissatisfaction with one’s skin tone. Affected individuals may be convinced that their complexion is consistently lighter than it truly is.
